name: Blockchain
summary: Networks that record and secure transactions
blurb: Shared ledgers with consensus—the settlement layer everything else sits on. Each article includes full explainers, key points, and tips.

items.title: Bitcoin
items.summary: The first peer-to-peer electronic cash network with fixed issuance rules
items.intro: Bitcoin shows how value can move on the internet without a bank as referee. A global set of nodes shares one ledger secured by cryptography and incentives. For beginners, keys, UTXOs, and issuance rules matter more than short-term price charts.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body:
Trusted intermediaries can freeze accounts, block payments, or fail in crises. Bitcoin replaces institutional permission with public verification: anyone can check the history, while rewriting it is designed to be extremely expensive.
The genesis block even embedded a newspaper headline about bank bailouts—an intentional signal about monetary rules in code.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body:
You sign a transaction that spends unspent outputs (UTXOs) to new addresses. Miners compete via proof-of-work to append blocks and earn rewards.
Halvings reduce new supply over time; difficulty adjusts so blocks remain roughly steady. More confirmations means lower reorg risk.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Private keys equal control; addresses can be public. Fees are a market for block space. Bitcoin’s scripting is intentionally limited, so it behaves more like settlement and digital scarcity than a general app platform.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Volatility is not a protocol bug. Coins on an exchange are IOUs until withdrawn. Phishing, fake support, and wrong-network transfers cause permanent losses—practice with tiny amounts first.

keyPoints: Bitcoin is a publicly verifiable settlement network, not a company token.
Issuance rules including halvings are enforced by the protocol and incentives.
UTXO + signatures define transfers; lost keys mean lost funds.
Security is mostly key hygiene and confirmation habits.
tips: Practice receive/send with a reputable or hardware wallet.
Move size in batches and wait for enough confirmations.
Back up the seed offline—never photograph or message it.
items.body: Bitcoin shows how value can move on the internet without a bank as referee. A global set of nodes shares one ledger secured by cryptography and incentives. For beginners, keys, UTXOs, and issuance rules matter more than short-term price charts.

items.title: Ethereum
items.summary: A general-purpose blockchain for smart contracts—often called a world computer
items.intro: Where Bitcoin focuses on transferring money, Ethereum focuses on enforcing programmable rules. Contracts custody assets, encode conditions, and compose into apps. After the Merge, consensus is proof-of-stake while execution remains the EVM.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body:
Payments alone cannot express loans, exchanges, or on-chain governance cleanly. A shared virtual machine turns code into public infrastructure.
Open interfaces let tokens and protocols plug into each other—the foundation of DeFi legos.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body:
EOAs are key-controlled; contract accounts are code-controlled. You pay gas for state changes. Validators stake ETH to propose and attest; severe faults can be slashed.
Users still interact via wallet signatures, but the design space is far wider than simple transfers.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Gas meters computation. Token standards (ERC-20/721) enable wallet and market compatibility. Layer 2 moves execution off mainnet while settling back to Ethereum’s security.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: “On Ethereum” ≠ audited or safe. Unlimited approvals and fake tokens drain wallets. Peak fees can exceed trade size—check network, contract, and allowance scope.

keyPoints: Ethereum is a shared state machine plus smart-contract runtime.
PoS secures consensus; the EVM executes applications.
Standards make assets interoperable across the ecosystem.
Safety depends on contract quality, approvals, and bridges.
tips: Verify contract addresses in a block explorer, not by ticker alone.
Use official L2s or wait when mainnet is congested.
Test new protocols with money you can afford to lose.
items.body: Where Bitcoin focuses on transferring money, Ethereum focuses on enforcing programmable rules. Contracts custody assets, encode conditions, and compose into apps. After the Merge, consensus is proof-of-stake while execution remains the EVM.

items.title: Consensus
items.summary: How a network agrees on one canonical history
items.intro: Without a central referee, nodes still need one ledger. Consensus defines who proposes blocks, how cheaters are punished, and when a transfer is final enough. Proof-of-work and proof-of-stake are different ways to make rewriting history costly.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body:
Distributed participants can delay, disconnect, or lie. Consensus prevents double-spends by making one history economically dominant.
For users, it determines wait times, reorg risk, and attack cost.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body:
PoW prices attacks with energy/hashrate. PoS prices attacks with bonded capital and slashing. Some protocols offer stronger finality after checkpoints; others are probabilistic.
Exchanges set deposit confirmations from these properties.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Liveness vs safety trade-offs matter. A “faster” chain with tiny validator sets may weaken censorship resistance. Ask who produces blocks before celebrating TPS.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Slogans are not investment theses. Bridge and light-client assumptions are often weaker than base consensus—and that is where many hacks land.

keyPoints: Consensus elects a single canonical history among untrusted nodes.
PoW and PoS price attacks differently.
Cross-chain components can be weaker than the L1 story.
tips: Respect suggested confirmation counts for large deposits.
Study validator distribution and slashing rules on new chains.
Reduce bridge/leverage activity during contentious upgrades.
items.body: Without a central referee, nodes still need one ledger. Consensus defines who proposes blocks, how cheaters are punished, and when a transfer is final enough. Proof-of-work and proof-of-stake are different ways to make rewriting history costly.

items.title: Accounts & Keys
items.summary: On-chain identity is a keypair, not a username reset by support
items.intro: Your account is usually an address derived from a private key. Nobody can reset that key for you; a signature is authorization. Understanding EOAs, contract accounts, and seed phrases is the foundation of safe use.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Web2 accounts live on company servers with password reset. Blockchains push control to key holders for self-custody—and push operational responsibility with it.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Private keys derive public keys and addresses. Seeds (BIP-39) can regenerate many accounts across chains. Contract accounts move funds by code paths; smart accounts encode policies like limits and guardians.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Hot wallets are convenient; hardware wallets keep keys in a secure element. Multisig spreads control. One leaked seed can compromise an entire derivation tree.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Cloud screenshots, malware, and “support” seed requests are classic loss paths. Blind signing can approve drains—reject unclear prompts.

keyPoints: Addresses are shareable; seeds are not.
EOAs are human-signed; contracts are code-controlled.
Read the permission scope before signing.
tips: Separate experiment funds from savings wallets.
Write seeds on paper/metal and store offline.
Enable transaction simulation on new dApps.
items.body: Your account is usually an address derived from a private key. Nobody can reset that key for you; a signature is authorization. Understanding EOAs, contract accounts, and seed phrases is the foundation of safe use.

items.title: Gas & Fees
items.summary: Every state change is metered so the public computer cannot be spammed for free
items.intro: Gas is not an arbitrary tax—it prices computation and storage. Your fee is usage × unit price. Congestion spikes the unit price, which is why the same action can cost cents or tens of dollars.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Public blockchains must bound resources. Gas creates a fee market: higher bids clear first; developers must write efficient contracts.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Simple transfers cost little gas; complex DeFi routes cost more. After EIP-1559, base fees burn and tips pay proposers. L2s amortize L1 data cost across many users, so unit fees drop.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Gas limit caps how much you allow. Failed transactions can still charge gas because execution happened. Speed-up/cancel replaces a pending nonce with a higher fee tx.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Fake sites may prompt absurd gas or nonsense calls. “Zero gas” campaigns often expand permissions—ask who sponsors and what you authorize.

keyPoints: Gas meters execution; price is market-driven.
L2s and batching are the main fee savers.
Reject abnormal fee or approval requests.
tips: Do non-urgent actions off-peak or on L2.
Use wallet fee estimates and simulation.
Price total gas before multi-step campaigns.
items.body: Gas is not an arbitrary tax—it prices computation and storage. Your fee is usage × unit price. Congestion spikes the unit price, which is why the same action can cost cents or tens of dollars.

items.title: Bridges
items.summary: Channels that move value or messages across chains—and a frequent hack target
items.intro: Assets do not magically appear on another ledger. Bridges lock, mint, burn, or swap via liquidity—expanding access while concentrating risk. Several of history’s largest exploits hit bridge custody and verification.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Without bridges, ecosystems stay islands. With bridges, users inherit extra trust and contract risk in exchange for mobility.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Models include lock-and-mint, burn-and-redeem, liquidity networks, and light-client relays. Canonical rollup bridges inherit rollup security but may have exit delays; fast bridges add third-party assumptions for speed.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Can you redeem 1:1? How decentralized are validators? High TVL can mean a fatter target, not automatic safety.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Phishing domains thrive around bridges. Wrong network or token contracts send funds into voids. Always test with a tiny transfer first.

keyPoints: A bridge is a cross-ledger protocol, not teleportation.
Canonical vs fast bridges have different trust models.
Verify domain, contract, and network together.
tips: Enter bridges from bookmarked official docs only.
Test minimal size before moving size.
Treat pending exits as not freely spendable yet.
items.body: Assets do not magically appear on another ledger. Bridges lock, mint, burn, or swap via liquidity—expanding access while concentrating risk. Several of history’s largest exploits hit bridge custody and verification.

name: DeFi
summary: Lending, swapping and staking via smart contracts
blurb: How open financial primitives compose—and the risks around rates, liquidations, and stables.

items.title: Automated Market Makers
items.summary: Liquidity pools and pricing curves replace classic order books
items.intro: AMMs let anyone deposit tokens into a pool so traders can swap against a formula. You get continuous liquidity and LP fees—plus impermanent loss and smart-contract risk.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: On-chain order books are costly. Pools keep liquidity resident in contracts so swaps can happen anytime, democratizing market making.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Constant-product is the classic curve; stableswaps and concentrated liquidity improve capital efficiency. Routers split trades across pools. Slippage limits protect you when state moves.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Impermanent loss can make LPs underperform holding. Fake tokens and honeypots can look buyable but unsellable. Emissions APRs may not last.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Unlimited approvals to unknown routers are dangerous. Depegs stress “stable” pools hard.

keyPoints: AMMs price via pool math for instant swaps.
LPs earn fees and take IL + contract risk.
Slippage and routing quality drive outcomes.
tips: Set tight slippage and minimum-out amounts.
Prefer deep pools on mature protocols.
items.body: AMMs let anyone deposit tokens into a pool so traders can swap against a formula. You get continuous liquidity and LP fees—plus impermanent loss and smart-contract risk.

items.title: Lending Protocols
items.summary: Overcollateralized borrowing with algorithmic rates and liquidations
items.intro: Deposit assets to earn yield or borrow against collateral without a credit desk. Health factors, oracles, and liquidation bots—not relationship managers—keep the system solvent.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: On-chain enforcement of unsecured credit is hard, so overcollateralization dominates. Anyone can participate; capital efficiency is the trade-off.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Utilization drives interest curves. Oracles feed prices. When health falls, liquidators repay debt and seize collateral for a bonus.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Isolation modes, LTV, and bad-debt socializations differ by protocol. Looped leverage multiplies risk. Net APR must subtract gas and liquidation penalties.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Oracle lag or manipulation can cause wrongful liquidations. Treating lending as “safe savings” is a mindset trap.

keyPoints: Oracle and liquidity quality decide safety.
tips: Leave a large buffer above liquidation.
Avoid highly correlated collateral in storms.
items.body: Deposit assets to earn yield or borrow against collateral without a credit desk. Health factors, oracles, and liquidation bots—not relationship managers—keep the system solvent.

items.title: Stablecoins
items.summary: On-chain units designed to track a stable reference like USD
items.intro: Volatile base assets are awkward for pricing and accounting. Stablecoins provide a dollar-like rail for trading and remittances—but mechanisms and failure modes differ sharply.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: They supply a familiar unit of account for on-chain activity and a temporary refuge in risk-off moments—refuge ≠ risk-free.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Fiat-backed coins rely on reserves and redemption; crypto-backed ones on overcollateralization; algorithmic designs adjust supply and have proven fragile. Transparency and redemption terms matter in stress.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Freezes, depegs, fake cross-chain versions, and yield wrappers add layers of risk. Same ticker on another chain may be unofficial.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: USD in the name is marketing, not insurance. Concentration in one issuer is counterparty risk.

keyPoints: Stablecoins are tools with issuer/mechanism risk.
Reserves, collateral, or algorithms fail differently.
Redemption and freeze policies affect usability.
Always verify official contracts per chain.
tips: Prefer transparent redeemable designs for size.
Treat outsized “stable yield” as a warning.
items.body: Volatile base assets are awkward for pricing and accounting. Stablecoins provide a dollar-like rail for trading and remittances—but mechanisms and failure modes differ sharply.

items.title: Staking & Restaking
items.summary: Bond capital to secure a network—and sometimes reuse that security
items.intro: Proof-of-stake aligns validators with chain security via bonded stake. Liquid staking tokens improve capital efficiency; restaking reuses stake for extra services and stacks correlated slashing risk.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: PoS needs a sufficiently decentralized validator set. Rewards compensate operations and opportunity cost; liquid staking raises participation with new contract risks.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Activation and exit queues, duties, and slashing define the job. Restaking delegates security to additional protocols for extra yield—and extra slash conditions.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Operator performance, client diversity, and LST depeg risk matter. Higher yield usually means more ways to be punished.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Fake staking sites harvest approvals or seeds. Restaking is not risk-free leverage on ETH.

keyPoints: Unstaking delays mean liquidity is not instant.
tips: Choose operators with track records and low concentration.
Enter only via official documentation links.
items.body: Proof-of-stake aligns validators with chain security via bonded stake. Liquid staking tokens improve capital efficiency; restaking reuses stake for extra services and stacks correlated slashing risk.

items.title: Perpetual Futures
items.summary: Non-expiring leveraged markets anchored by funding rates
items.intro: Perps let traders long/short with margin and no expiry. On-chain venues encode margin and liquidations in code or hybrid systems. Upside is amplified—so is path-to-zero speed.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Spot alone cannot express hedges efficiently. Perps became crypto’s dominant derivative by removing roll friction.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Funding transfers between longs and shorts to tether price to an index. Maintenance margin triggers liquidations; insurance funds may absorb shortfalls. Oracles and outages matter in chaos.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Leverage, auto-deleveraging, and funding accrual determine survival. CEX vs DEX custody models differ.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: “Small leverage is safe” fails in wicks. Inability to add margin because of gas/network issues can liquidate you.

keyPoints: Leverage converts volatility into wipeout odds.
Venue and oracle risk stack on market risk.
tips: Default to low leverage with spare margin.
Reduce size before events; don’t revenge-add.
Use venues whose rules you can verify.
items.body: Perps let traders long/short with margin and no expiry. On-chain venues encode margin and liquidations in code or hybrid systems. Upside is amplified—so is path-to-zero speed.

items.title: RWA Tokenization
items.summary: Bringing claims on real-world cashflows onto crypto rails
items.intro: RWAs connect familiar yields (like T-bills) to on-chain settlement. The token is only as good as legal wrappers, custody, and redemption—not just the smart contract UI.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Native crypto yield is volatile; tokenized cash instruments can better match treasury needs when structures are sound.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A licensed entity holds assets; tokens track claims; yield is distributed on-chain. KYC allowlists are common. Secondary prices can diverge from NAV.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Bankruptcy remoteness, attestations, T+N redemption, and jurisdiction decide stress outcomes. “Visible on-chain” ≠ automatically enforceable off-chain.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Counterparty and regulatory change risk sit beside contract risk. Fake subscription pages abound.

keyPoints: Diligence the issuer structure, not just APR.
tips: Read offering docs and reserve attestations.
Confirm your jurisdiction allows holding it.
Watch redemption windows and secondary depth.
items.body: RWAs connect familiar yields (like T-bills) to on-chain settlement. The token is only as good as legal wrappers, custody, and redemption—not just the smart contract UI.

name: NFTs
summary: Unique tokens and the marketplaces for them
blurb: From standards and markets to culture, games, and dynamic assets.

items.title: ERC-721 & ERC-1155
items.summary: Standard interfaces for unique and semi-fungible tokens
items.intro: Standards let wallets and markets speak one language. 721 maps one id to one owner; 1155 manages many ids and batch transfers—handy for games.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Without standards, every project invents bespoke APIs and breaks interoperability. Creators also gain multi-market distribution.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Ownership and transfers are standardized; metadata often lives at a tokenURI (commonly IPFS). Approvals can be per-token or operator-wide.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Mutable metadata, pinning, and royalty policy shape durability and economics. Fake collections copy art with different contracts—trust addresses.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Blind setApprovalForAll to unknown markets is a classic drain. Rarity narratives ≠ liquidity.

keyPoints: Standards enable interop, not intrinsic value.
Contract address is the authenticity check.
tips: Split high-value pieces across vault wallets.
items.body: Standards let wallets and markets speak one language. 721 maps one id to one owner; 1155 manages many ids and batch transfers—handy for games.

items.title: NFT Marketplaces
items.summary: Listing, bidding, settlement, and royalty policy layers
items.intro: Markets match buyers and sellers with on-chain or hybrid order flow. Aggregators route across venues. Royalty enforcement is increasingly marketplace policy, not pure protocol magic.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Creators need distribution; collectors need discovery and price formation. Competition compresses fees and raises security expectations.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Sellers approve transfers; buyers settle. Watch stolen listings at impossible discounts. Aggregators help price but not due diligence.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Fees, bid escrows, wash trading, and cross-listing quirks matter. Floor charts can be manipulated.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Phishing UIs mimic top markets. Airdrop signatures are a common lure.

keyPoints: Markets are rails, not value guarantees.
Ultra-low asks may be stolen assets.
tips: Bookmark official domains; skip search ads.
Keep bid size and expiry conservative.
items.body: Markets match buyers and sellers with on-chain or hybrid order flow. Aggregators route across venues. Royalty enforcement is increasingly marketplace policy, not pure protocol magic.

items.title: PFP & Culture NFTs
items.summary: Identity and community membership wrapped as tradable media
items.intro: Profile-picture NFTs turn ownership into a social signal. Pricing is narrative- and liquidity-driven more than cashflow-driven. Treat them as culture first, speculation second.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Platform usernames are rented; PFPs attempt portable visual identity and community access—attention can monetize, and attention can leave.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Mints, rarity tools, Discord/Telegram, and secondary trading form the loop. Some add utility; many do not.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Holder distribution, unlocks, and thin books drive crash risk. Impersonation scams are constant.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Chasing “blue chip” narratives at euphoria peaks hurts. Never trust DM admins with seeds.

keyPoints: Value is mostly social and narrative.
Collect/socialize; don’t treat as guaranteed yield.
items.body: Profile-picture NFTs turn ownership into a social signal. Pricing is narrative- and liquidity-driven more than cashflow-driven. Treat them as culture first, speculation second.

items.title: Game Assets
items.summary: Tradable items, characters, and land with verifiable ownership
items.intro: Crypto games promise that scarce items remain yours. Fun loops, balanced economies, and real ownership must coexist—or you are left with a speculative shell.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Traditional shutdowns wipe inventories. Open markets and verifiable ownership change player expectations and enable UGC economies.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Hybrids keep realtime combat off-chain and settle scarcity on-chain. Mints, sinks, and crafting shape prices; unchecked emissions inflate them away.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Production/sink ratios and spenders matter more than art alone. Ownable ≠ demanded.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Treating early token rewards as a salary fails in bear markets. Separate game keys from vault wallets.

keyPoints: Ownership needs a sustainable game loop.
tips: Isolate game accounts from main funds.
items.body: Crypto games promise that scarce items remain yours. Fun loops, balanced economies, and real ownership must coexist—or you are left with a speculative shell.

items.title: Tickets & Credentials
items.summary: Verifiable access rights with optional transfer rules
items.intro: Tickets and memberships are about proving entitlement. On-chain credentials can reduce fakes and enable controlled resale—if check-in UX actually works for normal people.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Paper fakes and opaque scalping hurt events. Verifiable digital tickets can bind identity or set transfer constraints and leave auditable trails.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Mint/claim on purchase; scan-to-redeem marks used. Soulbound options reduce touting. Privacy/KYC often sits off-chain.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Transferability, screenshot attacks, and recovery if seeds are lost all need design. Wallet friction can exclude audiences.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Fake ticket mints and abandoned events leave worthless tokens. Don’t overshare personal data to unknown contracts.

keyPoints: Value is the right, not the flip.
tips: Test wallet display before the event.
items.body: Tickets and memberships are about proving entitlement. On-chain credentials can reduce fakes and enable controlled resale—if check-in UX actually works for normal people.

items.title: Dynamic NFTs
items.summary: Assets whose traits can change with on-chain or oracle state
items.intro: Dynamic NFTs update appearance or attributes from game progress, time, or external data. They feel alive—but mutability must be transparent to buyers.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Membership tiers and evolving game items need state. Dynamics make NFTs more than static images.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Contracts or metadata services update URIs from triggers. If metadata is centralized, dynamics can become silent edits.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Who may update? Is history auditable? Marketplaces must show the latest state. Buyers should know what can change.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Operators could nerf rarity. Oracle faults can set wrong forms. “Immutable rarity” plus silent admin updates is a red flag.

keyPoints: Dynamics are a feature and a risk.
tips: Store high-value pieces in cold wallets.
items.body: Dynamic NFTs update appearance or attributes from game progress, time, or external data. They feel alive—but mutability must be transparent to buyers.

name: Layer 2
summary: Scaling networks built on top of Ethereum
blurb: Optimistic/ZK rollups, data availability, bridges, and why fees can fall to cents.

items.title: Optimistic Rollups
items.summary: Assume batches are valid; secure them with a fraud-proof window
items.intro: Optimistic rollups execute on L2, post data to Ethereum, and assume correctness unless challenged. Users get cheaper UX; canonical exits may wait out a challenge period.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: L1 block space is expensive. Moving execution off-chain while anchoring to L1 cuts costs. Optimistic designs shipped early with strong EVM compatibility.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A sequencer orders transactions and publishes batches; state roots anchor on L1. During the window, watchers can dispute. Fast exits use third-party liquidity with extra assumptions.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Sequencer decentralization, data availability, and upgrade keys define real security. UX speed ≠ finished decentralization.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Ignoring exit delays mis-prices liquidity. Fake bridge sites spike whenever L2s trend.

keyPoints: Challenge windows trade latency for simpler fraud proofs.
Security leans on L1 data + dispute games.
Canonical bridges are slower but clearer.
Sequencer uptime is an experience risk.
tips: Plan L1 exits with the delay in mind.
Read escape-hatch docs for sequencer outages.
items.body: Optimistic rollups execute on L2, post data to Ethereum, and assume correctness unless challenged. Users get cheaper UX; canonical exits may wait out a challenge period.

items.title: ZK Rollups
items.summary: Validity proofs convince L1 that L2 batches are correct
items.intro: Validity proofs let L1 accept results without long fraud windows. Proving is computationally heavy, but finality can feel snappier once proofs land.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Scale without relying on “assume honest unless challenged.” Faster settlement helps exchanges and bridges.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: L2 executes; provers build proofs; L1 verifiers check them. Higher EVM equivalence eases app migration.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Proof systems, DA, and upgrade keys still matter. “ZK” branding ≠ decentralized prover markets yet.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Centralized provers/sequencers can remain. Bridges and phishing still dominate user losses.

keyPoints: Hardware/engineering costs shape fees and decentralization.
Users still need bridge and wallet hygiene.
items.body: Validity proofs let L1 accept results without long fraud windows. Proving is computationally heavy, but finality can feel snappier once proofs land.

items.title: Data Availability
items.summary: Ensuring anyone can obtain the data needed to reconstruct state
items.intro: Rollups must make transaction data obtainable. If data vanishes, users may be unable to exit safely. Blobs lowered Ethereum DA costs and helped compress L2 fees.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Proofs without data can still trap users. Where data lives—and how costly it is—sits at the center of scaling debates.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Data can sit in Ethereum calldata/blobs or external DA layers, often with sampling/erasure coding. Security inheritance differs by design.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: “Settled to Ethereum” is not identical to “DA equals full Ethereum guarantees.” Fee drops often track cheaper DA.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Underestimating DA failure modes is dangerous. Marketing may blur settlement vs availability.

keyPoints: Blob-era upgrades changed L2 fee curves.
Judge fees, safety, and decentralization together.
tips: Don’t rank chains by TPS alone.
items.body: Rollups must make transaction data obtainable. If data vanishes, users may be unable to exit safely. Blobs lowered Ethereum DA costs and helped compress L2 fees.

items.title: L2 Bridges
items.summary: Canonical versus third-party paths between L1 and L2
items.intro: Canonical bridges inherit rollup rules and may be slow; third-party bridges sell speed with extra trust. Choosing the wrong UI is a top loss pattern.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: You need funds on L2 for cheap UX, or back on L1 for settlement. Different users pick different trust/latency points.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Official bridges credit L2 balances after deposit and exit per rollup rules. Fast bridges front liquidity and rebalance later—watch fees and limits.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Domain authenticity, upgradeability, caps, and refund paths matter. Faster usually means more counterparties.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Search-ad fake domains. Bridging the wrong token version strands liquidity. Spending funds still in challenge windows mis-marks risk.

keyPoints: Canonical bridges match rollup assumptions best.
Fast bridges trade trust for time.
tips: Click bridges from the L2’s own site.
Avoid unaudited brand-new bridges for size.
items.body: Canonical bridges inherit rollup rules and may be slow; third-party bridges sell speed with extra trust. Choosing the wrong UI is a top loss pattern.

items.title: Account Abstraction
items.summary: Smart contract wallets with recovery, limits, and sponsored gas
items.intro: Classic EOAs mean seed phrases and self-paid gas. AA lets wallets define verification logic—guardians, session keys, batching, paymasters—so onboarding feels closer to Web2 without fully giving up self-custody.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Seeds scare newcomers; gas tokens confuse them. AA reduces friction while keeping verifiable control. dApps gain fewer popups via sessions and batches.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: UserOperations are bundled on-chain; paymasters may sponsor fees. Wallet contracts enforce policies. Standards like ERC-4337 vary by chain maturity.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Who are guardians? Is recovery centralized? Are session permissions too wide? Misconfig still loses funds.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: “No seed” ≠ no risk—recovery channels can be attacked. Malicious bundler/paymaster endpoints exist. Sessions to unknown dApps are dangerous.

keyPoints: AA encodes policy in contract wallets.
Sponsored gas and social recovery are headline UX wins.
Phishing still works if you approve blindly.
items.body: Classic EOAs mean seed phrases and self-paid gas. AA lets wallets define verification logic—guardians, session keys, batching, paymasters—so onboarding feels closer to Web2 without fully giving up self-custody.

items.title: Multi-chain Reality
items.summary: Liquidity and users fragment across many settlement domains
items.intro: Few people live on one chain now. Gas tokens, bridges, and app deployments differ. Intent solvers hide paths, but you still must know where funds sit.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: One chain cannot optimize every fee/performance niche. More choice also means more ways to pick the wrong network.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Wallets switch RPC/chain ID; the same address can hold different assets per EVM chain. Bridges and messaging connect states; solvers compete to fill intents.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Chain ID authenticity, fake RPCs, and per-chain token contracts are daily footguns. Zero balance often means wrong network selected.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Malicious custom RPCs trick signatures. Bridging windows add risk. Spreading irreplaceable funds across ten new L2s is operational debt.

keyPoints: Intents hide complexity; they don’t erase bridge risk.
tips: Label networks clearly in your wallet.
Learn exits before depositing into a new chain.
items.body: Few people live on one chain now. Gas tokens, bridges, and app deployments differ. Intent solvers hide paths, but you still must know where funds sit.

items.title: Why L2 Fees Can Be Cents
items.summary: Batching and cheaper data amortize L1 costs across many users
items.intro: On congested L1 you bid for scarce block space. L2s pack many txs together so each user pays a slice of shared data/proof cost—often down to cents.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: High fees block micropayments and game loops. Lower fees let normal people use apps, not just watch charts.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Execution happens on L2; summaries hit L1. Blob-era DA cuts unit costs. L2s can still congest, usually far below L1 peaks. Bridge fees and slippage are separate line items.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Cheap ≠ equally decentralized. Sequencer fee policy shapes UX. Multi-step approvals still add up.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Risking a bridge scam to save two dollars is irrational. Stress events worsen both fees and exit times.

keyPoints: Amortization + cheaper DA drive fee compression.
L2 congestion exists at a different scale.
Total cost includes bridge, slippage, and time.
tips: Include bridge fees when comparing routes.
Wait out spikes for non-urgent actions.
Keep a little L1 ETH as escape fuel.
items.body: On congested L1 you bid for scarce block space. L2s pack many txs together so each user pays a slice of shared data/proof cost—often down to cents.

name: Infrastructure
summary: Oracles, storage, indexing and developer tools
blurb: The invisible pipes that power wallets, DeFi, and safer UX.

items.title: Oracles
items.summary: Bridges that bring off-chain facts into smart contracts
items.intro: Contracts cannot see exchange prices or real-world scores alone. Oracles aggregate external data for liquidations, perps, and insurance. When they fail, cascades follow.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Blockchains isolate for determinism, yet finance needs inputs. Oracles balance freshness with integrity—without them most DeFi stops.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Sources aggregate, outliers drop, updates push on a heartbeat or demand. Some designs stake and slash bad reporters. Circuit breakers matter in chaos.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Thin markets are easier to manipulate for bad loans. Cross-chain messages are oracle-like trust problems too.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Having “an oracle” ≠ invulnerability. Stale prices, wrong decimals, and paused feeds all bite.

keyPoints: Judge sources, aggregation, and update rules.
Illiquid assets are easier to spoof.
Protocol circuit breakers reduce blast radius.
tips: Know which feed and heartbeat a protocol uses.
Reduce precision-sensitive actions in extreme volatility.
items.body: Contracts cannot see exchange prices or real-world scores alone. Oracles aggregate external data for liquidations, perps, and insurance. When they fail, cascades follow.

items.title: RPC & Nodes
items.summary: How wallets read chain state and broadcast transactions
items.intro: Wallets talk to blockchains through RPC endpoints. Public RPCs are easy but may rate-limit, log, or be swapped for phishing. Understanding RPC helps debug “wrong balance” and stuck txs.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Not everyone runs a full node. RPCs expose node capabilities as APIs while preserving the option to self-host.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Apps send JSON-RPC calls to query state or send raw txs. Providers differ on archive depth, privacy, and reliability.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Malicious RPCs can show fake balances or censor txs. Signing stays local, but bad data can still trick you. Verify chain IDs when adding networks.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: One-click “add network” from shady sites is risky. Public outages are not always wallet bugs. Never commit RPC secrets into public frontends.

tips: On weird balances, switch nodes or use an explorer.
items.body: Wallets talk to blockchains through RPC endpoints. Public RPCs are easy but may rate-limit, log, or be swapped for phishing. Understanding RPC helps debug “wrong balance” and stuck txs.

items.title: Indexers
items.summary: Turning raw logs into queryable product APIs
items.intro: Scanning the whole chain for every UI is slow. Indexers ingest events into databases so portfolios and leaderboards feel instant—most “history” views come from indexes, not live full scans.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Products need filtered queries at internet speed. Analysts and bots rely on the same layer.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Define a schema, process logs, store, serve GraphQL/REST. Outages show stale UI. Decentralized indexer networks incentivize multiple operators.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: UI can lag true chain state. Upgrades require indexer updates. Don’t liquidate based on a dashboard alone—verify on-chain.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Corrupt indexes mislead traders. Phishing “portfolio” sites mimic real dashboards.

keyPoints: Indexes speed queries; they are not consensus.
Explorers/contracts are source of truth for critical moves.
Indexer faults look like protocol bugs.
tips: Serious monitoring can read nodes directly.
items.body: Scanning the whole chain for every UI is slow. Indexers ingest events into databases so portfolios and leaderboards feel instant—most “history” views come from indexes, not live full scans.

items.title: Decentralized Storage
items.summary: Content-addressed networks for files and NFT metadata
items.intro: Storing large files on L1 is pricey, so media often sits on IPFS/Arweave-like systems. Hashes ensure integrity, but online availability still needs pinning or paid permanence.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Central servers can delete NFT media. Decentralized storage improves durability and censorship resistance for apps and datasets.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Files get content IDs; nodes retrieve by hash. IPFS needs pinning; some networks emphasize pay-once permanence. HTTP gateways help browsers but add gateway trust.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Mutable centralized tokenURIs undermine the story. Back up important metadata hashes.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: “On IPFS” ≠ immortal if nothing pins it. Malicious gateways can inject scripts. Verify hashes before running binaries.

keyPoints: Content addressing prevents silent edits, not neglect.
Mutable admin URIs are a red flag.
tips: Pin metadata for high-value NFTs yourself.
items.body: Storing large files on L1 is pricey, so media often sits on IPFS/Arweave-like systems. Hashes ensure integrity, but online availability still needs pinning or paid permanence.

items.title: MEV
items.summary: Value extractable from transaction ordering and inclusion
items.intro: Builders and searchers can reorder or insert txs—sandwiches, liquidation races, and more. Users feel it as toxic slippage; protocols respond with auctions and private flow.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Public mempools expose large swaps to predators. Understanding MEV explains slippage settings and private submission options.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Searchers find opportunities; builders pack blocks; proposers publish. Some chains redistribute MEV to stakers. Sandwiches wrap your trade to worsen price.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Slippage caps, private relays, batch auctions, and intents mitigate harm. L2 sequencers can extract MEV too.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Not every bad fill is MEV—wide slippage is self-inflicted. Avoid sketchy “anti-MEV” extensions.

keyPoints: MEV comes from orderable public flow.
Users mitigate via slippage and private paths.
Treat it as an engineering reality.
tips: Split large swaps and tighten slippage.
Avoid huge market orders in peak chaos.
items.body: Builders and searchers can reorder or insert txs—sandwiches, liquidation races, and more. Users feel it as toxic slippage; protocols respond with auctions and private flow.

items.title: Developer Tooling
items.summary: Testing frameworks, libraries, and account kits that raise the safety floor
items.intro: Ecosystem safety depends on Foundry/Hardhat-style tests, typed libraries, simulation, and account kits—not auditors alone. Better tools catch bugs earlier and help wallets explain signatures.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Manual deploys fail. Untested contracts are time bombs. Front-end SDKs unify multi-chain connection and error handling.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Forked tests, fuzzing, deploy scripts, monitoring, and AA SDKs form the loop. Pre-sign simulation shows asset diffs.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Stale dependencies carry known CVEs. Supply-chain attacks hit “safe” packages. Users should prefer clear-signing wallets.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Copy-pasting unaudited samples to mainnet is reckless. Fake “dev tools” extensions steal keys.

keyPoints: Clear signing reduces user phishing success.
tips: Install extensions only from official sources.
items.body: Ecosystem safety depends on Foundry/Hardhat-style tests, typed libraries, simulation, and account kits—not auditors alone. Better tools catch bugs earlier and help wallets explain signatures.

items.title: On-chain Identity
items.summary: Readable names, attestations, and reputation for human coordination
items.intro: Long addresses are easy to mistype. Name systems map human labels to records; attestation protocols issue claims like membership. Usability rises—and so do privacy and impersonation issues.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Payments and social need memorable handles. Names reduce transfer mistakes and act as Web3 business cards. Reputation helps anti-Sybil with privacy trade-offs.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Register a name, set records, optionally gather signed attestations. Some credentials are soulbound.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Names expire; records change. The same string may resolve differently across chains. Separate identity addresses from vaults.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Impersonation domains steal funds. Binding every credential to one doxxable address overexposes you.

keyPoints: Names are a resolution layer, not a bank guarantee.
Always check resolved addresses before sending.
Attestations help coordination with privacy costs.
Split public identity from vault addresses.
tips: Use a low-value address for public socials.
items.body: Long addresses are easy to mistype. Name systems map human labels to records; attestation protocols issue claims like membership. Usability rises—and so do privacy and impersonation issues.

items.title: Bundlers & Paymasters
items.summary: Backend rails that package UserOperations and sponsor gas
items.intro: Without bundlers, UserOperations struggle to land; without paymasters, gas sponsorship and “pay with any token” are hard. Misconfigured AA infra becomes outage or abuse surface.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Users dislike holding every chain’s gas token. Apps want to sponsor first actions. Infrastructure enables those product policies with budgets and allowlists.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Wallets build UserOperations; bundlers simulate and submit; EntryPoint executes; paymasters fund per policy with rate limits.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Is sponsorship bound to certain contracts? Can it be farmed? Will bundlers censor? Decentralization affects resilience.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Malicious endpoints and leftover wide sessions after campaigns are risks. Gasless ≠ approval-less.

keyPoints: AA UX depends on reliable bundlers/paymasters.
Endpoint choice affects privacy and censorship.
items.body: Without bundlers, UserOperations struggle to land; without paymasters, gas sponsorship and “pay with any token” are hard. Misconfigured AA infra becomes outage or abuse surface.

name: Wallets
summary: Apps and devices that hold your keys
blurb: Hot/cold wallets, seeds, multisig, and custody models explained.

items.title: Hot Wallets
items.summary: Connected software wallets for everyday small balances
items.intro: Browser and mobile wallets make dApps instant. Convenience expands attack surface: malicious sites, fake extensions, clipboard malware, lost phones. Treat them as checking accounts, not life savings.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Cold wallets are clumsy for high-frequency DeFi. Hot wallets teach signing and network switching quickly.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Keys sit encrypted on device; unlock locally; broadcast via RPC. Connecting a dApp shares an address, not the key—yet dangerous signatures still drain.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Split spend vs savings accounts. Review allowances. Biometrics protect the app unlock, not chain recovery.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Sideloaded APKs, seed “sync” pages, and public computers are classic fails.

tips: Use a dedicated browser profile for crypto.
items.body: Browser and mobile wallets make dApps instant. Convenience expands attack surface: malicious sites, fake extensions, clipboard malware, lost phones. Treat them as checking accounts, not life savings.

items.title: Hardware Wallets
items.summary: Keys in a secure chip with on-device confirmation
items.intro: Hardware wallets keep private keys off the infected PC. You still must read the device screen—blind signing or shady firmware can beat the best chip.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Long-term and large holdings need stronger isolation. Physical confirmation raises the bar for remote theft. Teams use them as baseline vault controls.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: The host builds a tx; the device shows a summary; you approve; the signature returns for broadcast. Seeds generated at init are the backup. Firmware updates must be official.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Buy authentic devices; know blind-signing policies per chain. Losing the device is fine if the seed is safe; losing the seed is not.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Tampered second-hand devices, “checker” websites asking for seeds, and OK-without-reading are failure modes.

keyPoints: Hardware isolation blocks many remote key thefts.
Screen verification is still on you.
Seed backup equals the device in importance.
Supply chain and firmware hygiene matter.
tips: Test with tiny transfers after setup.
Match full addresses on-device for size.
items.body: Hardware wallets keep private keys off the infected PC. You still must read the device screen—blind signing or shady firmware can beat the best chip.

items.title: Seed Phrases
items.summary: Human-readable backups that regenerate wallet keys
items.intro: 12/24 words are not a login password—they are the master secret that recreates keys. Anyone with the words can empty wallets elsewhere. No real support agent needs your seed to “verify” you.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Devices die. Seeds let you restore the same accounts elsewhere in an offline-writable form.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: BIP-39 turns entropy into ordered words that derive accounts. Wrong order fails restore. Optional passphrases add security and forgetfulness risk.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Photos, cloud sync, and chat are unsafe. Metal backups beat paper against fire/water. Multi-location backups must balance theft vs total loss.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Phishing “wallet sync” pages and fake support are top killers. Typing a seed into any website is an emergency.

keyPoints: Design redundancy against both fire and theft.
tips: Never store in photos or email.
items.body: 12/24 words are not a login password—they are the master secret that recreates keys. Anyone with the words can empty wallets elsewhere. No real support agent needs your seed to “verify” you.

items.title: Multisig
items.summary: Shared accounts that require M-of-N approvals
items.intro: Multisig turns “one phish loses all” into “several people must agree.” Ideal for treasuries and families. It cuts single points of failure and adds coordination overhead.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Single-key vaults die in one mistake. Multisig forces attackers to compromise multiple signers and encodes separation of powers.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A contract or native scheme sets threshold and owners. Propose → collect signatures → execute. Signer rotation and modules need equal care.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Diverse devices beat correlated malware. Too-high thresholds brick funds; too-low thresholds weaken security. Emergency modules can be backdoors.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: All signers on one hot browser, never rehearsing recovery, and phishing the Safe UI are common fails.

keyPoints: Multisig spreads key and decision risk.
Threshold design sets availability vs safety.
items.body: Multisig turns “one phish loses all” into “several people must agree.” Ideal for treasuries and families. It cuts single points of failure and adds coordination overhead.

items.title: Smart Accounts
items.summary: Programmable wallets with limits, guardians, batching, and sessions
items.intro: Smart accounts encode policy: daily limits, allowlists, recovery, and batch calls. More flexibility than EOAs—and more ways to misconfigure modules.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: EOAs are all-or-nothing. Smart accounts enable everyday low privilege with high-value extra scrutiny, bridging toward seedless UX.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Logic lives in a contract with pluggable validators, often paired with AA bundlers/paymasters. Module upgrades must be guarded.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Least privilege, audits, and tested recovery paths matter. Know who can upgrade before calling it a vault.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Random unaudited plugins, naive guardians, and believing smart accounts stop all phishing are mistakes.

items.body: Smart accounts encode policy: daily limits, allowlists, recovery, and batch calls. More flexibility than EOAs—and more ways to misconfigure modules.

items.title: Custody Models
items.summary: Whoever holds the keys effectively controls the assets
items.intro: Custodians trade password reset and support for counterparty risk. Self-custody trades sovereignty for personal ops risk. Most people mix both: trade on platforms, save in wallets.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Different goals need different risk models. Pure self-custody scares beginners; pure custody hurts in platform failures.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Custodial balances are often internal ledgers until withdrawal. Self-custody broadcasts every move. Regulated custodians may attest reserves—still not zero risk.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Freezes, queues, jurisdiction, and proof-of-reserves quality matter. Self-custody failures look like lost seeds and bad signatures.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: “Too big to fail” has failed repeatedly. Storing a seed in an exchange notebook is not self-custody.

keyPoints: Convenience vs sovereignty is the trade.
tips: Practice self-custody with small size first.
items.body: Custodians trade password reset and support for counterparty risk. Self-custody trades sovereignty for personal ops risk. Most people mix both: trade on platforms, save in wallets.

name: Gaming
summary: Games and virtual worlds with owned assets
blurb: Gameplay, economies, infrastructure, and speculative failure modes.

items.title: Play & Own
items.summary: Fun first, verifiable ownership as a bonus—not a wage illusion
items.intro: Healthy crypto games prioritize entertainment; ownership amplifies, it does not replace design. Secondary markets should be outcomes, not the only content.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Pure speculation collapses in bears. Embedding ownership in genuinely fun loops improves retention and enables creator economies.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Core gameplay runs fast off-chain or on specialized rails; scarce settlements hit a chain. Studios earn via UX, fees, and services while tuning economies.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Retention and spend metrics beat token charts as health signals. Regulation can still constrain item tokens.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Treating grind as a job and ignoring account security are classic traps.

keyPoints: Healthy economies balance sinks and sources.
tips: Read economy notes and patch history.
items.body: Healthy crypto games prioritize entertainment; ownership amplifies, it does not replace design. Secondary markets should be outcomes, not the only content.

items.title: In-game Economies
items.summary: Issuance and sinks decide whether item prices can stand
items.intro: Open economies behave like tiny fiscal systems: endless emissions without sinks collapse prices. Reading production vs destruction beats listening to GameFi slogans.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Open trading removes some studio control, forcing more serious design so long-term players and traders can coexist.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Quests emit; crafting/repairs/seasons sink; dashboards reveal inflation. External token prices shock internal loops.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Dual tokens, energy, and land rents can help or confuse. Watch team unlocks and market-maker wallets.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Early high yields attract mercenaries, not players. Copying economics without an audience fails.

items.body: Open economies behave like tiny fiscal systems: endless emissions without sinks collapse prices. Reading production vs destruction beats listening to GameFi slogans.

items.title: Virtual Worlds
items.summary: Ownable land and social space narratives
items.intro: Virtual land sells location, traffic, and presence. Some worlds host ongoing activity; others stall after sales. Judge by builders and DAUs, not cinematic trailers.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: People want durable digital commons and storefronts. On-chain ownership enables secondary markets and experiments by brands.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Land NFTs plus clients plus optional rentals. Content comes from users or officials; performance often relies on traditional servers.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Foot traffic sets land value. Empty worlds are speculative art. Building rights and royalties shape creator willingness.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Primary-sale FOMO and treating metaverse slides as short-term yield are traps.

items.body: Virtual land sells location, traffic, and presence. Some worlds host ongoing activity; others stall after sales. Judge by builders and DAUs, not cinematic trailers.

items.title: Game Infrastructure
items.summary: Engineering trade-offs between low latency and on-chain settlement
items.intro: Action games need millisecond feedback. Studios use authoritative servers plus on-chain scarce assets, or specialized high-throughput chains. Knowing the trust boundary prevents “fully decentralized” marketing confusion.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Pure L1 loops are too slow/expensive for many genres. Layering keeps playable UX with verifiable scarcity.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Matchmaking/combat off-chain; mints/trades/jackpots on-chain. Anti-cheat stays largely off-chain. Appchains raise throughput but add bridge/liquidity costs.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Which parts trust a server? Do assets survive a studio shutdown? That defines how real “ownership” is.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: “Fully on-chain” claims with mutable server truth. Bridging game assets via fake sites.

keyPoints: Latency and decentralization pull opposite ways.
tips: Move meaningful assets to self-custody wallets.
items.body: Action games need millisecond feedback. Studios use authoritative servers plus on-chain scarce assets, or specialized high-throughput chains. Knowing the trust boundary prevents “fully decentralized” marketing confusion.

items.title: Modding & UGC
items.summary: Creators earn when maps, skins, and mods can settle transparently
items.intro: UGC extends game life. If mods are tradable with clear splits, creators show up. On-chain splits aid auditability; IP licensing still decides whether it scales.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Traditional UGC faces sudden platform policy shifts. Open markets and programmable royalties offer another incentive path and richer player content.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Creators publish assets → markets trade → contracts split revenue. Moderation and discovery decide whether quality concentrates.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: License scope, content policy, and chargebacks remain. On-chain math does not auto-settle lawsuits.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Buying unauthorized brand mods and volatile creator tokens are risks.

keyPoints: UGC needs clear IP and revenue rules.
tips: Cash out with personal risk limits.
items.body: UGC extends game life. If mods are tradable with clear splits, creators show up. On-chain splits aid auditability; IP licensing still decides whether it scales.

items.title: Speculative Game Risk
items.summary: When fun depends on rising prices, bear markets break the loop
items.intro: Failed projects treat token pumps as content. Players become mercenaries, economies turn reflexive, and maintenance stops when price falls. Spotting the pattern saves tuition.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Risk education is part of a healthy product: communities that discuss inflation honestly outlast hype discords.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: High emissions attract entry → sell pressure rises → price falls → players leave. The break often appears when incentives cut. Few titles successfully pivot to real games.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Is revenue mostly new entrants? Is the team shipping playable updates? Secondary price is not a fun metric.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: FOMO hostage phrases and leveraged grinding are danger signs.

tips: Ask: would I play at zero token price?
items.body: Failed projects treat token pumps as content. Players become mercenaries, economies turn reflexive, and maintenance stops when price falls. Spotting the pattern saves tuition.

name: DAOs
summary: Communities that govern with on-chain votes
blurb: Governance, treasuries, proposals, legal wrappers, and attack surfaces.

items.title: Token Governance
items.summary: Votes that set parameters, upgrades, and spending
items.intro: DAOs push upgrades and treasury decisions to token holders or reputation systems. One-token-one-vote is simple and whale-prone; delegation and other designs try to improve representation. Voting power is influence—and an attack surface.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Protocols must change without becoming a single-company dictatorship. On-chain votes leave auditable trails and can constrain teams.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Proposal → discussion → vote → timelock → execution. Delegation lets small holders entrust experts. Quorums and vetoes blunt low-turnout captures.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Distribution, treasury size, and timelock length matter. Airdropped voters may be apathetic. Forum mood can diverge from on-chain results.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Flash-loan votes (if allowed), bribes, and voting unread are risks.

keyPoints: Mechanism design fights whales and apathy.
Read impacts and conflicts before voting.
items.body: DAOs push upgrades and treasury decisions to token holders or reputation systems. One-token-one-vote is simple and whale-prone; delegation and other designs try to improve representation. Voting power is influence—and an attack surface.

items.title: DAO Treasuries
items.summary: Shared on-chain capital for building, liquidity, and buffers
items.intro: Treasuries are DAO ammunition. Diversification, transparency, and spending process decide whether they are runway or honeypots. Multisigs or governors control payouts the community should audit.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Public goods need funding for audits, builders, and incentives. Treasuries keep value under community-visible control and can stabilize crises.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Inflows from fees/issuance/financing; outflows via proposals. Holdings may mix stables, majors, and native tokens—native concentration is reflexive risk.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Runway months, FX risk, and address inventories matter. Soft commitments count too.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: All-volatile treasuries and opaque related-party spending are red flags.

items.body: Treasuries are DAO ammunition. Diversification, transparency, and spending process decide whether they are runway or honeypots. Multisigs or governors control payouts the community should audit.

items.title: Proposal Lifecycle
items.summary: From forum draft to on-chain execution
items.intro: Good proposals debate off-chain, temperature-check, vote on-chain, then execute after a timelock. Surprise “lightning proposals” are a smell. Know which stage you are in.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Process replaces either dictatorship or chaos, giving opponents time to organize and inserting audit/legal review where needed.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Draft → feedback → final text → vote → queue. Failed ideas can revise. Some systems use gasless off-chain signatures for voting.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Quorum, thresholds, and emergency paths matter—overbroad emergencies are backdoors. Executable calldata must match the text.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Title-only voting and ignoring timelock alerts are failures.

tips: Restate risks in your own words before voting.
Verify execution matches the proposal text.
items.body: Good proposals debate off-chain, temperature-check, vote on-chain, then execute after a timelock. Surprise “lightning proposals” are a smell. Know which stage you are in.

items.title: Legal Wrappers
items.summary: Foundations and companies that interface DAOs with the off-chain world
items.intro: Code does not automatically grant limited liability. Foundations/LLCs sign contracts, bank, and tax. Contributors should know who may be treated as responsible if things break.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Hiring, IP, and regulators need legal counterparts. Good wrappers reduce personal exposure—they are not cloaking devices.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Jurisdiction → charter → board/multisig → clauses linking to DAO votes. Rules vary wildly by country.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Securities, sanctions, and taxes (including airdrops) matter. Anonymity ≠ zero legal risk.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Assuming “decentralized” ignores local law, or signing unknown agreements, is reckless.

keyPoints: Compliance is part of product risk.
tips: Seek professional advice for material contributions.

items.title: DAO Operations
items.summary: Turning votes into shipping via working groups and payouts
items.intro: Without operators, governance is theater. Working groups, bounties, budgets, and reviews convert energy into product. Burnout, unclear ownership, and late payrolls kill DAOs quietly.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Public goods are under-supplied. Ops systems fund maintenance; transparent pay reduces shadow deals.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Mission → metrics → budget → hiring/bounties → retros. On-chain payroll helps. Least-privilege admin access avoids single points of failure.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Are KPIs verifiable? Is double-dipping controlled? Documentation fights bus factor.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Paying without accountability and overloading irreplaceable contributors are failure modes.

keyPoints: Budgets and performance should be public.
tips: Start with small bounties to learn process.

items.title: Governance Attacks
items.summary: Capturing protocols via votes, bribes, or low turnout
items.intro: Attackers chase treasuries, parameters, or upgrade keys using accumulated votes, flash loans, bribes, or sleepy quorums. Defenses include timelocks, veto guardians, and better voting designs.

sections.heading: What problem it solves
sections.body: Discussing attack surfaces lets communities defend early. “Nobody would do that” is not a control. Governance security rivals contract security.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Acquire votes → pass malice → execute after timelock if unstopped. Complex parameters can camouflage intent. Guardians may delay or cancel clear attacks.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.body: Snapshot timing, flash-loan voting rules, and delegation concentration are key. Monitor large token movements.

sections.heading: Risks & misconceptions
sections.body: Ignoring timelock alerts and assuming audits stop governance theft are mistakes.

keyPoints: Governance power can become direct theft.
tips: Support designs that block flash-loan voting.
